verses.note: Spiritual gifts, even real ones, are not proof of a saving relationship with Christ. Paul says the same of prophecy and miracles without love (1 Corinthians 13:1-3).

Christians disagree about whether such signs continue. Cessationists, following B. B. Warfield (Counterfeit Miracles, 1918), hold that miraculous gifts marked the apostolic age and ceased with it; Pentecostal and charismatic Christians hold that the gifts continue. Both sides agree that the signs serve the word and are never a way of forcing God to act, and that a promise of protection is not a command to seek danger (Matthew 4:7).

The first gift of the Spirit in Acts is speech about God's works in languages the speakers did not know. Christians differ on whether the tongues of 1 Corinthians 12-14, which needed interpretation, are the same gift, and on whether such gifts continue today; the chapter note sets out the main positions.

The gift named is prophecy, speech from God, given to daughters and maidservants as well as sons and menservants. Luke shows women prophesying (Luke 2:36, Acts 21:9). How this bears on women's roles in the church's offices is a second-order question on which faithful churches differ.
A spiritual gift is given for others' strengthening, not for the giver's status. Even an apostle's gift works both ways in the church, a principle Paul develops in 12:3-8.

Miracles were a present reality in the Galatian churches, and Paul attributes them to God's continuing supply of the Spirit to people of faith. The gifts are not earned by law-keeping; they flow from the same grace that justifies.

The gifts of the Spirit are distributed by God's will, not earned or demanded. Churches differ on whether such signs continue today in the same form (continuationists) or chiefly accompanied the apostolic foundation (cessationists), and this verse, which speaks of confirmation of the first witnesses, is cited on both sides.
